title: Oona and the Wobbly Strawberry
markdown:
Oona the hedgehog was a master of order. From her snug home by the old oak she looked after the most important thing in the school garden: the noticeboard. Not any board — a way for everyone to share news. Every morning, tiny sharp pen in dark berry juice, she crafted announcements. Handwriting so neat each letter was a little curl, a wave on a calm sea. Whisperwood gathered, whiskers wiggling, ears like flags. “Oona’s notices,” Kit the fox would say, tail wagging, “are little poems for the eyes. They make everything clear.”

Today her neat world had sprung a wobbly leak. Mr. Field, kindest badger, paws soft as moss, heart warm as toast, had grown the most magnificent strawberry for the Harvest Festival: a true king among berries, ruby-red, plump as a robin’s egg after a cozy night, smelling of sunshine mixed with the sweetest happiness. She had even swept the earth around its stem so no leaf dared look sloppy. Oona scanned the garden this morning and her prickles stood on end, a sure sign. The special spot she had kept spotless was bare. Utterly, alarmingly, wonderfully bare — which was the worst kind of wonderful.

Prickles shivered to her tippy-toe paws. Everything must be just so, in its place. The empty space felt like a wobbly tooth in a straight row, a cloud on a blue sky. Her biggest trouble was things not in their rightful places, the world messy and unpredictable. Her tummy filled with fluttery butterflies bumping into each other.

“Oh dear, oh dearie.” Mr. Field would be disappointed; he always had such a cheerful round face. The Harvest Festival, best party of the year, would be less without his prize jewel. She pictured little animals looking sad. That would not do.

“Right then.” She puffed her small round chest. “I shall fetch it back.” She hopped from the perch and trotted to the garden gate. New territory. Usually: neat pumpkins, pruned bushes, swept paths. Beyond: woods a little too wild, rustling, dark spots.

The path was narrower than she liked, winding like curly string. Twigs caught fur. Sunlight made messy patches through leaves. Prickles felt not quite right. Then brambles, a tangled ball of thorny yarn chewed by an energetic kitten. Disorder prickled like a hundred tiny needles, the same tangle as her morning tummy. Whiskers drooped. She almost turned back to the predictable board.

A deep voice rumbled, startling a robin. “Lost? You look as out of place as a snail in a squirrel race.” A badger larger and gruffer than Mr. Field blocked the path, serious wrinkled face, tummy rumbling. Oona felt like a fallen acorn beside a giant tree. Big, overwhelming, a little grumpy. “I am looking for a very special strawberry.” He grunted, pebbles rolling. “No strawberries here. Roots and grubs, and a hungry badger.” He nudged a sharp bramble. “Go now, before you get snagged.”

She took a shaky breath, remembered Mr. Field’s smile and the joy his strawberries brought, and nudged carefully past, heart a tiny drum, through the thorns, whispering apologies to snagged leaves. The festival and that hopeful face pushed her on.

Deeper in, trees tall, shadows dancing, a tiny happy rustling. Through a curtain of ferns: a family of field mice snuggled around something wonderfully red and round. Mr. Field’s giant strawberry. Not stolen. Rolled, perhaps nudged by a playful breeze. The mice were nibbling, whiskers wiggling, squeaks filling the air.

Her heart squeezed. Joy, just not in the expected place. Then the festival, Mr. Field’s possible sadness. Prickles heavy with what-should-be. Paws froze on damp earth. If she gave them this, the festival berry would be incomplete. What if he thought her careless? What if everyone was disappointed? Fur tingled. She breathed damp soil, nudged the remaining part. It teetered, rolled with a soft thump toward the mice. A chunk of planned order bounced away. Leaves rustled. The sweet scent went bittersweet. Shared happiness, at a cost she could name later.

With the remaining half balanced on her back she walked out lighter. Kit waited at the gate, tail thump-thump-thump on the post. “You found it!” Together they set it in a woven basket and returned it to Mr. Field, worried-hopeful. Oona, Kit steady beside her, penned a new notice in her clearest hand: how the strawberry had rolled, found a hungry family, and how a happy piece had been shared.

Creatures gathered to read. A gentle spreading warmth, not the old flutter. The garden was still beautiful, still cheerful, with a slightly smaller strawberry. Later, sun setting orange and pink, something small and bright peeked under a plump white daisy: a tiny wild strawberry, no bigger than her littlest toe, vibrant red, a little crooked, a little wild, certainly not perfect, still a strawberry, bright and promising. She smiled, untroubled, to her eyes.

She logged bare-spot / bramble-badger / mice-half / wild toe-berry in the notice book in her neatest berry-juice curls, left the board a space for festival thanks, and let Kit wag at the daisy as if foxes judged fruit. Mr. Field read the notice twice and smiled with the remaining half, which was still a jewel. The world, she decided, was a bit like that wild strawberry — not always in its place, not always as expected, and full of the sweetest surprises if you carried half a prize home and told the truth about the other half.
